body.objective: Students will be able to mix colours and build a value scale in paint.
body.iCan: I can mix colours and build a value scale in paint.
successCriteria: I can mix secondary and tertiary colours from primaries
I can build a value scale with tints and shades
I can use complementary or analogous colours on purpose in a composition
body.hook: Painters can make a red apple glow, a sky feel cold or a shadow feel full of colour, all with only a few tubes of paint. The secret isn't buying more colours. It's knowing how to mix them and how to control light and dark.

vocabulary.definition: The name of a colour, such as red, blue or yellow-green.
A hue mixed with white to make it lighter.
A hue mixed with black or its complement to make it darker.
Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel, such as red and green.
Colours next to each other on the colour wheel, such as blue, blue-green and green.
How light or dark a colour is.
How the parts of an artwork are arranged.

study.title: Colour Wheel and Value Studio
study.question: How do painters control colour and value?
study.passage:
Materials: acrylic or tempera paint in red, yellow, blue, white and black; brushes; palette; water; heavy paper.
Part 1, Colour wheel (20 minutes): Paint a 12-part wheel. Start with the primaries (red, yellow, blue), mix the secondaries (orange, green, violet), then the tertiaries (red-orange, yellow-green and so on). Add small amounts of the darker colour to the lighter one.
Part 2, Value scale (15 minutes): Choose one hue. Paint a nine-step scale: four tints (add white), the pure hue, and four shades (add black on one side; on a second strip, darken with the complement instead and compare).
Part 3, Colour schemes (10 minutes): Paint two small thumbnails of the same simple scene (for example a mug on a table): one with a complementary scheme, one with an analogous scheme.
Part 4, Reflect (5 minutes): Which scheme feels calmer? Which feels more energetic? Why?
Tip: Darkening with the complement gives richer shadows than black, which can make colours look muddy.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson; colour theory summarized from standard art education sources.
steps: Mix primaries into secondaries and tertiaries
Compare darkening with black and with the complement
Reflect on the mood of each scheme
discussion: Which mixes were hardest to get right, and why?
How does darkening with the complement change a shadow?
How could you use a colour scheme to lead the viewer's eye?
study.product: Paint a small still life using either a complementary or analogous scheme, with at least five values, and write two sentences explaining your colour choices.

steps: Shade: add black or orange (the complement)
examples.answer: Light blue is a tint; navy is a shade

practice.q: What are the three primary colours in painting?

practice.a: A colour darkened with black or its complement.
How light or dark a colour is.

practice.q: What is the complement of red?
Mix red and yellow. What secondary do you get?
Name a tertiary colour and how to mix it.
practice.a: Blue-green: mix blue and green (other tertiaries accepted).

practice.q: What is an analogous colour scheme?
practice.a: Three or more colours next to each other on the wheel.

practice.q: Why add dark paint to light paint a little at a time?
practice.a: Dark colours are stronger and quickly overpower the mix.

practice.q: What happens when you mix complements in equal amounts?
practice.a: You get a neutral brown or grey.

practice.q: Why does a value scale matter in painting?
practice.a: Value creates form, depth and contrast.

practice.q: Why might an artist darken with a complement instead of black?
practice.a: It gives richer, more natural shadows; black can make colours muddy.

practice.q: How could colour lead the viewer's eye to a focal point?
practice.a: Put the strongest contrast or a complementary accent at the focal point.

practice.q: Compare the mood of a complementary and an analogous scheme.
practice.a: Complementary feels energetic and high contrast; analogous feels calm and unified.

practice.q: A painting looks flat. Suggest two fixes.
practice.a: Increase the value range, add warm-cool contrast or stronger shadows.

misconceptions: Thinking black is the best way to darken every colour
Thinking more colours of paint means better paintings
Thinking value only matters in drawing, not painting
exitTicket: Mix and name one tertiary colour.
Explain why complementary colours create contrast.

test.title: Practice test: Mix colours and build a value scale in paint

items.q: Which colours are primaries in painting?
items.answer: B) red, yellow, blue

items.q: Adding white to a hue makes a
items.answer: D) tint

items.q: The complement of blue is
items.answer: B) orange

items.q: Value describes
options: A) the size of a shape
B) the name of a colour
C) how light or dark a colour is
D) how bright a colour is
items.answer: C) how light or dark a colour is

items.q: Mixing yellow and blue makes
items.answer: C) green

items.q: An analogous scheme uses colours that are
options: C) next to each other on the wheel
items.answer: C) next to each other on the wheel

items.q: Mixing two complements together makes
options: A) a neutral brown or grey
items.answer: A) a neutral brown or grey

items.q: Red-orange is a
items.answer: A) tertiary colour

items.q: Why add dark paint to light paint gradually?
options: B) Dark pigment quickly overpowers a mix
items.answer: B) Dark pigment quickly overpowers a mix

items.q: Which choice best creates a focal point?
options: B) using the same value everywhere
C) placing the strongest contrast at the centre of interest
items.answer: C) placing the strongest contrast at the centre of interest

items.q: A shadow painted with black looks dull. A better choice is
items.answer: D) mixing in the complement

items.q: A calm, unified mood is most likely with
items.answer: B) an analogous scheme

items.q: Name the three secondary colours.
items.answer: Orange, green and violet.

items.q: What is a shade?
items.answer: A hue darkened with black or its complement.

items.q: How do you mix a tertiary colour?
items.answer: Mix a primary with a neighbouring secondary.

items.q: Explain what a complementary colour scheme is.
items.answer: Colours opposite each other on the wheel, used together for contrast.

items.q: Why is a value scale useful?
items.answer: It shows the range of light to dark to create form and contrast.

items.q: Describe the mood of a warm analogous scheme.
items.answer: Warm, energetic or cozy (answers vary with reasons).

items.q: Plan a colour scheme for a stormy landscape and explain it.
items.answer: Answers vary; for example cool analogous blues and greys with high value contrast for drama.

items.q: Explain how colour and value together create depth.
items.answer: Warm, high-contrast colours come forward; cool, low-contrast colours recede.
